h: Demanding dignity: young people change the language of protest
dek: Sudhir Kumar Suthar sees movements as a new way of practising citizenship, alongside making demands.
body: Young people are taking to the streets for more than jobs or a fair examination result. They are also challenging how they are treated. Sudhir Kumar Suthar argues that seeing recent protests as a collection of separate grievances misses their larger point: people want to live with dignity and be able to speak their minds.

Suspected cheating in examinations, a lack of school toilets, women's insecurity and uncertain employment are different experiences. According to the writer, they are connected by the belief that citizens deserve better lives. For many young people, attending a demonstration, sharing someone's video or speaking in their support is therefore becoming a civic responsibility.

The methods of this politics matter as much as its demands. Familiar posters and flags now appear alongside memes, reels and spontaneous replies. The writer sees these experiments as efforts to reach others, change social understanding and practise democracy in one's own conduct. He also draws attention to restraint, mutual care and the presence of women and queer people.

Suthar does not see this as complete disillusionment with institutions. In his reading, young people are demanding answers from the very institutions they want to trust. Government denial and repression have failed to understand this change, but the opposition has also lagged in grasping its depth. The movement's gains must be sought not only in an immediate resignation but also in citizens recognising their own rights and strength.
nazar: The demand for dignity will be met only when Dalits, minorities, women and the least-heard workers can speak as equals within the movement itself. The presence of young people is not in itself evidence of that equality.
Both the government and the opposition will be judged by concrete answers: whose grievance was heard, which procedure changed and who had to make the same rounds again to claim their rights.
sawal: Whose voice is heard least in the protest?
ref: Civic dignity
The right to live with equality and respect, and to speak one's mind in public life.
Prefigurative politics
Practising the equality and democracy one demands through one's own behaviour while seeking change.

h: On both sides of the border, power shows the same fear
dek: In Delhi's protests, Munah Khan recognises Pakistan's familiar repression and familiar courage.
body: Munah Khan read Amitava Kumar's post sharing his article directly after his Substack link would not open in India. This small episode reminds her of Pakistan's internet shutdowns and restrictions. Writing about Delhi's young people, she turns the mirror towards her own country too, where citizens have grown used to finding such workarounds.

The choice of the name cockroach has particular importance in her article. Adopting a name used to belittle someone as one's identity can reverse a relationship of fear. Memes, posters and laughter bring into public view things that major media platforms suppress. In Pakistan too, satire has found routes through closed doors.

Khan places the role of small digital journalists in this context. When major channels look away, people working with fewer resources and less protection create a record of events. This work matters in both countries, but these people also bear more of the risk. The article shows regional similarities rather than celebrating one country's victory over the other's distress.

Alongside this hope comes her warning. Laughter can keep a movement alive, but it cannot guarantee change. The state has time, money and the power to repress. The distance between India's democratic identity and Delhi's blockade troubles her. Looking from next door also means recognising the same questions in one's own society that are concealed while counting others' weaknesses.
nazar: Comparisons between India and Pakistan are often spent proving that the other country is worse. This article offers a more useful test: how much of the right to dissent remains at home?
It would be wrong to dismiss laughter, but assuming it will bring lasting change without organisation, legal assistance and accountability would also be premature.
sawal: Who will build a path to change after the laughter?
ref: Digital shutdown
Blocking access to the internet or an online platform, potentially affecting news, communication and livelihoods.
photo_note: Historical painting of Hooghly, used symbolically

h: A majority is no exemption from questions
dek: Tahir Kamran distinguishes an electoral mandate from institutional independence and the right to protest.
body: Tahir Kamran reads India's recent protests as a test of democracy. Regular elections matter, but he says they do not determine how fearlessly citizens can question those in power. Detentions in Delhi, restrictions on movement and the spread of the youth movement reveal where the relationship between an electoral mandate and civil liberties is tested.

The article preserves an important distinction in the dispute over electoral rolls. Removing duplicate or ineligible names is a legitimate administrative task for the Election Commission. But if eligible voters are excluded, transparency, fairness and an effective route of appeal become essential. Keeping the Commission's defence separate from critics' concerns, Kamran says trust will come from answers that can be checked.

He does not call a long period in office inherently undemocratic. The danger arises when personalised leadership reduces institutional independence and turns criticism into hostility towards the nation. In this connection, the writer raises questions concerning Arundhati Roy, Apoorvanand and the freedom of universities. These voices may make different arguments, but no government should stand above public scrutiny.

The article does not conclude that the movement has decisively weakened the government. It asks readers to watch the next concrete outcomes: whether detainees receive due process, whether voters can appeal and whether the Commission provides credible answers. For the writer, restoring citizens' belief that institutions and leaders must answer questions matters.
nazar: The strength of this analysis lies in its caution. It avoids treating a protest crowd as an election result or a complete restoration of democracy.
For us, the real accounting concerns those without lawyers, documents or money for repeated office visits. Having a right of appeal on paper and being able to exercise it are different things.
sawal: Who will hear the appeal of someone without documents?
ref: Due process
Safeguards such as notice before action, an opportunity to present one's case and a fair hearing.

h: Blocking the crowd, deepening the anger
dek: R. Prasannan asks what Delhi Police gained by closing avenues for peaceful protest.
body: R. Prasannan questions the handling of protests in Delhi. He gives examples from Britain and the United States where police made room for marches, spoke with protesters or avoided heavy riot-control deployment. For him, these examples show that protecting public order and hearing citizens' voices can happen together.

He then shows the difference between the treatment of opposition leaders' scheduled programmes and that of young protesters in Delhi. Restrictions, some ritual gestures and detention brought the leaders' protests to a close. But blocking roads and the Metro, deploying large forces and detaining leaders on arrival before the 10 October demonstration sent a very different message, in the writer's view.

He argues that such a blockade increases anger rather than ending protest. The next day, people sat down wherever they were stopped, and the protest spread. The article argues that giving citizens space to voice grievances peacefully is not a sign of weak government. Closing that space can make encounters between police and the public more confrontational.

Prasannan's satire targets the theatrical politics of both leaders and administrators. But its central question is serious: if lawful avenues of protest are continually narrowed, how will society express its anger? He argues for an arrangement in which the police also make demonstrations possible and safe, rather than simply blocking their path.
nazar: Police success cannot be measured solely by how many people they stop. Fewer injuries, less fear and space to voice grievances are also measures of public safety.
The same test applies to every state and every government. An opposition party being in office does not make stopping demonstrations in a city more acceptable.
sawal: Who is responsible for keeping a demonstration safe?
ref: Peaceful assembly
The constitutional right to gather publicly and express one's views without violence.

h: Anger on the streets, an uncertain election in UP
dek: Swaminathan Aiyar sees political possibilities in the movement but avoids predicting the outcome.
body: Will Delhi's youth protest affect the Uttar Pradesh election? Swaminathan Aiyar considers this an open question. He argues that a movement that began with examination grievances is now raising questions of electoral transparency and democratic accountability. The administration's anxious response could give it a larger political identity instead of suppressing its message.

The article distinguishes the Election Commission's claims from those of its critics. The Commission cites deceased, relocated and untraceable voters among the names removed; critics fear eligible people, particularly minorities, may have been excluded. Aiyar does not take manipulation of electoral rolls as proven. For him, unanswered questions about transparency have political importance in themselves.

He considers both the BJP's reduced Lok Sabha seats in Uttar Pradesh in 2024 and its subsequent recoveries in other assembly elections. Strategies such as better booth management, social alliances and cash assistance for women have helped the party return. It would therefore be unwise to treat one Lok Sabha result as a direct prediction of the next assembly election.

The article sets out several possibilities: the BJP could improve its position, a close contest like that of 2024 could return, or separate grievances could come together to give the opposition new strength. The youth movement opens the third possibility; its impact cannot yet be measured. There is time before the election, and alliances and the government's response will matter. Sensing unrest and becoming certain of a change in power are different stages.
nazar: Reading this article as a prediction would erase its own caution. People visible in a movement are not a representative sample of the entire electorate.
We must see whether grievances about unemployment, caste inequality and voting rights develop into a shared organisation and a lasting programme in villages.
sawal: The anger is shared. Is the programme shared too?
ref: The gap between votes and seats
Because victories are decided in separate constituencies, even a small change in votes can make a large difference in seats.

h: A blockade backfires, and the movement faces its own test
dek: Coomi Kapoor questions the changing strategy of protest alongside the government's mistakes.
body: According to Coomi Kapoor, disproportionate police deployment and restrictions on movement to stop Delhi's youth demonstration became bad publicity for the government. Instead of an ordinary protest being managed, the capital appeared besieged, and those images travelled abroad. She contrasts this with Mumbai's example of peacefully allowing space for a demonstration.

Social media is another important front in her column. Young protesters changed the direction of the conversation with quick replies, memes and the language of civil rights. This helped an already disheartened opposition. Questions about police conduct also emerged. Kapoor reads this as a sign that the administration initially lacked clear political understanding and a plan of action.

But her support is not unconditional. She says there is no certainty that a new call to hoist the national flag in restricted areas, going beyond demands that won public sympathy, will receive the same support. Amid the festivals, the movement's strategy and its public meaning will face a test. While criticising those in power, the article does not exempt protesters' next steps from scrutiny.

The column also connects opposition unity, Rahul Gandhi's relationships with student leaders and the politics of delimitation. The demand for Gyanesh Kumar's resignation has brought different opposition groups closer on one issue. But its assessments of party relationships and internal discussions are the journalist's reporting and interpretation. Its central point is that the movement must keep its direction clear to turn the advantage gained from government mistakes into lasting political trust.
nazar: Questions of rights and the usefulness of a particular strategy should be examined separately. While the right to peaceful protest remains, its organisers can also be questioned about their aims, preparation and safety.
Civil rights are larger than either the government's popularity or the movement's popularity. They cannot be left to either side's immediate convenience.
sawal: Who will turn support into lasting trust?
ref: Delimitation
The process of determining electoral constituency boundaries and the distribution of representation.

h: Change the faces in power, and strengthen citizens too
dek: Shailendra Chauhan looks beyond a change of government to everyday equality and institutional accountability.
body: Why do so many citizens' lives stay the same even when governments change? Shailendra Chauhan's article explores what systemic change means through this question. Removing a government hostile to the public is an essential democratic route, but a change of faces does not automatically change the distribution of resources, respect and opportunities. The next government may also work within those same relationships.

The article argues that the system cannot be found only in Parliament or the cabinet. Who receives education, who can access treatment, how secure work is and who is heard when policy is made are all part of it. Understanding economic inequality separately from caste and social deprivation misses major barriers to equality.

Chauhan also questions the idea that a majority grants the right to act arbitrarily. After winning an election, a government must respect the Constitution, independent institutions and dissent. Parliament, courts, universities and the media must scrutinise government decisions as well as carry them forward. If institutions weaken, democratic culture can shrink even while elections survive.

The article opposes keeping citizens as passive spectators between elections. Change should be measured against the actual lives of the most vulnerable: workers' safety, farmers' incomes, children's education and Dalit citizens' equality. Simply assuming a new person will be better is insufficient too. Politics must be structured so that scrutiny of power and citizens' participation in decisions keep increasing.
nazar: The movement faces a useful but difficult question: will success be measured by an officeholder's departure or by a change in procedures that help citizens?
A programme for equality must be visible in budgets, public services and institutions. Broad slogans can be tested only when accompanied by concrete demands and an accounting of work.
sawal: Whose lives will be used to measure change?
ref: Power relations
Who holds decisions, resources and influence in society, and who can question them.

h: Music's shared world, religion's dividing walls
dek: Ramachandra Guha sets music's mixed inheritance against today's communal politics.
body: Ramachandra Guha's article recalls a world of Hindustani music where relationships of learning and creation have crossed religious boundaries. An old encounter with a young singer in Pakistan surprises him, because a raga there was being set apart as belonging to Hindus. Against this, he offers examples of Muslim singers who embraced compositions with Hindu imagery.

Letters musicians wrote to Gandhi in 1944 are one focus of the article. Omkarnath Thakur wanted to expand music education at Banaras Hindu University. Violinist Parur Sundaram Iyer sought support, describing music as a means of Hindu-Muslim unity. In these letters, Guha sees an idea of national culture built jointly by different traditions.

Teacher-student relationships make this shared heritage more concrete. The relationships between Alladiya Khan and Kesarbai Kerkar, and Allauddin Khan and Ravi Shankar, show how one musician's achievement also includes the dedication of another community. N. Rajam and Bismillah Khan's duet, and the example of Sheikh Chinna Moulana from the south, bring this mixed world to life more vividly than any slogan.

Guha does not stop at praising the past. He says Partition damaged this shared world, and there are now signs in India too of music being confined to a majority religious identity. He worries about artists' conduct and the political effects of state patronage. His appeal is that we should not rest content with treating musical diversity as an inheritance; it must also be protected through today's choices and institutional conduct.
nazar: The strongest evidence of shared culture is not just harmony visible on stage, but equality in learning, employment and patronage too. We must ask how open opportunities are to less famous artists.
Giving ragas communal identities diminishes all the work generations have done by learning from one another.
sawal: The ragas are shared. Are the stages open to everyone too?
ref: Guru-shishya tradition
Learning an art from a master through long practice and close guidance.

h: Without equality in love, how can democracy have it?
dek: Mrinal Pande reads patriarchy at home alongside hatred in public life.
body: Mrinal Pande refuses to treat love as merely a matter of private relationships. Her article connects hatred in public life today, the treatment of women and young people's demands. She asks how fully a society can claim democratic equality and compassion when domination over women and children at home is considered normal.

She draws attention to the growing aggression associated with love in popular films, songs and social behaviour. Treating love across religions or freely chosen relationships with suspicion, and monitoring women's public presence, appear to her as forms of the same crisis. The article presents these tendencies as the writer's political and cultural assessment.

The language of respecting women as mothers, sisters and daughters does not automatically increase their freedom. Pande highlights the gap in a society that worships a goddess but will not accept a living woman's wishes, clothing or anger. Speeches about safety and empowerment can ring hollow when attempts are made to discipline the very woman who speaks.

The article sees the strength to declare their own freedom in young women's new slogans. It connects love with consent, dialogue and acceptance of another person's dignity. Family, Parliament and court decisions thus cease to be separate worlds. Alongside a language of defeating opponents, a democratic society needs a language in which people can listen, disagree and live together as equals.
nazar: The language of love is useful only when it accepts another person's wishes. Taking someone else's decisions into one's own hands in the name of care is not equality.
The same applies to the state. Claims of affection for citizens must be proven by hearing their questions and protecting their freedom to choose.
sawal: When does care become control over another person?
ref: Patriarchy
Social relationships and rules that make men's authority seem normal and limit women's freedom.

h: Why remember colonial humiliation but not caste humiliation?
dek: Mohit Nirmender questions the limited space for Dalit and Adivasi experiences in national memory.
body: Jallianwala Bagh is part of a shared memory of national humiliation and resistance. But why do the experiences of people denied water, education and respect because of caste not become part of the whole society's memory in the same way? Mohit Nirmender does not see this gap as merely a lack of historical knowledge. For him, it is a question of deciding whose hurt we consider our own.

The article brings together examples involving water rights, caste humiliation and education. Across different periods and social positions, a person's identity at birth can be placed before their civic rights. Even when the law grants equality, everyday conduct can withhold it. The writer links this gap to social memory.

He argues that experiences excluded from shared history become easier to ridicule. Turning the long history of being denied water into an anti-reservation taunt is one such example. Homes, schools and public culture teach children what to take pride in and whose grievances to dismiss as exaggerated.

Nirmender questions the repeated treatment of caste violence and humiliation as merely private tragedies. Colonial oppression offers an external culprit; remembering caste injuries demands confronting injustice within one's own society. The article insists that both our historical memory and our ability to recognise others' pain must change if the Constitution's equal dignity is to become a reality in public life.
nazar: Leaving the story of caste aside as a separate Dalit concern keeps the debate on equality incomplete. We can ask where this history appears in schoolbooks, museums and public events.
Building shared memory does not mean erasing differences in experience. First, we must hear the voices of those who suffered that humiliation.
sawal: Whose hurt is missing from our national memory?
ref: Mahad Satyagraha
The movement led by Ambedkar in 1927 for Dalits' equal access to public water.

h: Tear gas cannot erase questions about the cost of living
dek: Oliver Haynes records different sources of anger and the police response at protests in Paris.
body: Oliver Haynes did not encounter a uniform crowd on the streets of Paris. Students angry about failing schools, people demanding funding for public education, workers and citizens troubled by rising prices had come together. His article begins with the experience of tear gas, but asks why the crowd's grievances should be reduced to a picture of disorder.

He records both the peaceful march and the violence that followed. He does not conceal burning cars, damaged shops or bottles thrown at police. At the same time, he clearly says he did not see who started the initial confrontation. Distinguishing police action, protesters' different intentions and some people's violence is an important part of this report-like commentary.

Complaints about education and fuel costs meet memories of the earlier Yellow Vest movement in the article. The writer says repeated riot-control measures affect peaceful people too, and fear can turn to anger. Images of violence push the original demands into the background, while political parties begin giving those images their own meanings.

Haynes observes both right-wing leader Marine Le Pen's language of restoring order and the left's efforts to give the movement political direction. He warns the government that police can clear a route while budget and living-cost questions remain unresolved, but cannot end the crisis. If there is less space to hear grievances, another eruption will remain possible.
nazar: Opposing violence and demanding police accountability can go together. An attack on a shop does not end a student's right to demand a better school.
The lesson for India is the same: giving everyone in a crowd a single identity is easy; answering their different grievances is difficult but necessary.
sawal: How long can peace last without hearing grievances?
ref: Yellow Vest movement
Widespread protests in France that began in 2018 over fuel prices and the cost of living.

h: Before an agreement, the broken ground of trust
dek: Mahjoob Zweiri sees past experiences and the sequence of steps as factors in failed Iran-US talks.
body: Why do talks between Iran and the United States keep breaking down? Mahjoob Zweiri says reading the terms of proposals alone is not enough. Both governments come to the table carrying the weight of past experiences with each other. Washington wants Iranian action and verification first; Tehran first wants guarantees and relief from pressure that the next US government cannot reverse.

The article traces the roots of this distrust to the American-British role in overthrowing Mohammad Mossadegh's government in 1953 and the 1979 US embassy hostage crisis. The two events affect the two countries' political memories differently. The writer sees these memories not as the sole cause of current policy, but as a deep structure that prevents trust from forming in negotiations.

The US withdrawal from the nuclear agreement in 2018 increased Iranian suspicions. Zweiri reads recent wartime conditions and proposals against this background. He says the actual distance on several demands has narrowed somewhat, but a deadlock remains over who takes the first step and what they receive in return, and when. The sequence of negotiations has itself become a question of political security.

The article considers the attempt to give both sides some assurances in the June memorandum of understanding in Islamabad a useful example, even though it did not last. Zweiri concludes that another list of conditions will not suffice. A third-party guarantee is needed to make action and reciprocal action credible on both sides at the same time. This is his analysis drawn from history, not a claim that the next talks will succeed.
nazar: Instability in the Gulf also affects Indian families whose livelihoods depend on maritime trade and migrant work. The debate on peace must therefore centre citizens' safety alongside governments' prestige.
The language of trust will become concrete only when accompanied by clear routes for verification, implementation and accountability for violations.
sawal: Who will reduce the risk of taking the first step?
ref: JCPOA
The 2015 Iran nuclear agreement, which provided sanctions relief in return for restrictions on the nuclear programme.
photo_note: Landscape with a cactus, representative painting

h: Homes saving seeds, keeping choices open for the future
dek: Anushka Gurung and Sonam Yangchen Bhutia explore the links between knowledge, biodiversity and livelihoods in Sikkim's seed preservation.
by: Anushka Gurung and Sonam Yangchen Bhutia
body: The phrase seed bank brings to mind a large scientific storehouse. Anushka Gurung and Sonam Yangchen Bhutia show another system found in Sikkim's homes. Walls, roofs, platforms above the hearth and bamboo winnowing trays all help save seeds for the next sowing. This knowledge grew from farmers' needs and has been tested over generations.

Corn cobs are tied and hung in the air, while some vegetable seeds are spread out to dry. A wood-and-bamboo platform above the hearth is called a bhar. Its warmth and smoke help dry materials. The article describes traditional methods; it presents the idea that smoke repels pests as a local belief.

Different vegetables, spices and medicinal plants grow together in home gardens. This provides food while also keeping a collection of seeds and knowledge of their uses alive. The writers see seed preservation as a relationship between family, community and land, rather than a single technique. Seeds and the knowledge surrounding them travel between generations and villages.

Growing dependence on high-yield hybrid crops risks the loss of local diversity. The article goes beyond treating old methods merely as cultural mementos. It argues that locally adapted crops and the knowledge of how to preserve them keep future options open. In a region facing food insecurity, respecting community conservation is also connected to better farming and the ability to cope with a changing climate.
nazar: Praising local knowledge should not mean denying farmers better public support. Reliable access to seeds, water, healthcare and markets is essential too.
The claim of conservation will be fulfilled only when farmers and the women managing this household work participate equally in deciding which seeds to save.
sawal: Who will recognise the value of seed keepers' knowledge?
ref: Agricultural biodiversity
The different crops, varieties and associated living systems used in farming.
Kothe bari
A garden near the home where plants for food and other needs grow together.

h: Parents demanding justice for Sahil detained
dek: The Mooknayak records allegations by the family and activists about a protest outside IIT Bombay and police action.
body: A month after IIT Bombay student Sahil Wakode's death, Mumbai Police detained his parents and other protesters demanding justice on 18 October. According to The Mooknayak's report, Rahul Sonpimple and Deepali Salve were among those protesting near the institute's gate. Different people were taken to different police stations.

Salve alleged that women protesters were dragged, beaten and mistreated. The report records these statements as activists' allegations. They should not be read as findings of an independent inquiry. After news of the police action, appeals were also made for lawyers and other activists to reach the stations.

Sahil was a student in the Department of Energy Science and Engineering. He died on 18 September. His family alleges that he faced caste discrimination and harassment. Following his father's complaint, an FIR was registered against a professor for abetment of suicide and under the SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act. The Mumbai Police Crime Branch is investigating the case.

The family had been on hunger strike at Azad Maidan for several days, demanding accountability from the institute. The report also mentions earlier protests and detentions. A complaint being registered, an investigation being under way and someone being proven guilty are different stages. The latest incident has raised questions both about an impartial inquiry into a caste grievance at a university and about the public space available to a family and students seeking justice.
nazar: The allegations must be examined impartially in the investigation. Complaints about police conduct during the protest must likewise remain open to inquiry.
If a family must repeatedly go between the streets and police stations for answers about their child's death, the usefulness of institutional grievance systems comes into question.
sawal: When will the family's complaint receive a credible answer?
ref: SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act
A law to prevent caste atrocities against Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe people and protect victims.

h: Jamia students demand a union as action against protesters is questioned
dek: Students sought the restoration of elected representation, withdrawal of disciplinary action and the chief proctor's resignation.
body: In a statement issued on 18 October, Jamia Millia Islamia students repeated their demand to restore the students' union. According to Maktoob's report, students say the absence of an elected union since 2006 has deprived generations of a representative body through which to raise grievances. The current protest also involves a hunger strike and allegations that students were removed from campus.

The statement criticised the administration over the events of 17 October. Students allege that protesters were forcibly removed and security staff beat those on hunger strike. The report attributes these allegations to students. Holding the chief proctor responsible, students also demanded the proctor's resignation.

Their other demands include the immediate restoration of the students' union, withdrawal of existing disciplinary action connected to the movement and no further such action. Representatives of different student organisations asked the university to hold talks. They say treating students' participation as a matter of administrative convenience or a special concession lies at the root of the current dispute.

The report also recounts earlier efforts and the history of the demand reaching court. There was a hunger strike in 2017; the university later cited obstacles such as a pending case. A public interest petition concerning elections was disposed of in December 2022. This background shows that the current protest is not a demand that arose suddenly. Clear answers are still needed on all three matters: elected student representation, the hearing of grievances and the administration's legal position.
nazar: Treating a students' union as an enemy of discipline does not make everyday university questions disappear. There should be an answer about the regular, safe route through which students can speak.
Both the administration's response to allegations about the action and an impartial inquiry are necessary. The debate over elected representation cannot be reduced to a campus clash.
sawal: Through which elected forum can students speak?
ref: Students' union
An elected student representative body that takes questions about education, facilities and rights to the administration.

h: Delhi questioned, but protest restricted in Bengaluru too
dek: Around 50 people were detained at an anti-SIR protest near Town Hall; police cited an order governing protest locations.
body: Police detained around 50 people who gathered against SIR near Town Hall in Bengaluru on 17 October. According to The Indian Express report of 18 October, they included AISA members and social activists. The protesters opposed the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and demanded Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.

Police took people in two buses to the City Armed Reserve grounds on Mysuru Road. They were released after some time. Heavy police deployment and barricades surrounded Town Hall. The report says additional units remained there afterwards to prevent fresh protests. Traffic was also affected for a while during the gathering and deployment.

The police position is that Karnataka High Court directions allow protests and rallies only at Freedom Park. A notice dated 17 October cited a ban on protests, rallies and displaying placards at other locations. Organisers were told they could hold their event at Freedom Park after obtaining permission and complying with applicable conditions.

Organisers and activists called the restriction a double standard. They asked how a state government that criticised the blocking of peaceful demonstrations in Delhi was protecting the same right in its own city. The report presents both the police's legal argument and activists' objections. Alongside the protest's demands, the dispute concerns how readily citizens can find space to express their views.
nazar: The right to protest cannot change according to the party governing a state. Both the need for rules designating locations and the fairness of their use should be examined.
Simply releasing people does not fully answer why a peaceful assembly was stopped in the first place.
sawal: Will the freedom to protest change with the government?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, in which names and eligibility are checked again.

h: A shared call to save a temple in Dera Ismail Khan
dek: Amid fears of demolition at the Ramlila temple, civic groups and the Hindu community demanded an inquiry and protection.
body: Civic groups protested fears that the historic Ramlila temple in Pakistan's Dera Ismail Khan was being demolished for commercial construction. According to Dawn's report of 18 October, officials closed and sealed the building in Rahim Bazaar on Saturday. A few days earlier, civic activists' intervention had halted demolition work there.

Civil society representatives and Hindu community members held a meeting criticising the proposed construction. The meeting took place at Sohail Ahmed Azmi's office. Participants included Kishore Kumar, a former provincial legislator and Hindu community representative, and other local residents. They asked elected representatives to raise the matter in the National Assembly.

According to meeting participants, the Ramlila temple is among around 400 buildings in the city identified as cultural heritage. They expressed concern that no work damaging such a place should take place. Traders, writers and heritage conservation workers also called it a matter of the city's shared history.

Participants questioned the permission granted by the relevant officials and their legal authority. This allegation is their position; the report does not establish it as a final legal finding. They called for complaints to be taken to the district administration, archaeology department and other relevant forums, and demanded an inquiry. Sealing the building has stopped work immediately, but demands for clear answers about its ownership, conservation and future use remain.
nazar: Protecting a minority community's heritage is the whole city's responsibility. The coming together of different groups in this case matters.
Sealing a building is no substitute for permanent conservation. Only clear legal status, repairs and public oversight will secure the historic building's future.
sawal: Who will take responsibility for the temple's lasting protection?
ref: Cultural heritage
Buildings and traditions connected to history and community life whose protection has public importance.
photo_note: Historic view of Vrindavan, representative painting

h: Mass arrests after protests in France put pressure on government
dek: The Guardian's live report of 18 October details violence and police action alongside demands over schools and rising prices.
body: After major demonstrations and violence on 17 October, France's government held crisis meetings on 18 October. The Guardian's live report quoted Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez giving a figure of 1,800 arrests. A later correspondent's report on the same page put the number above 2,000. It would be unwise to treat changing figures as a settled final count.

Rising living costs have now joined grievances that began with teacher shortages, dilapidated buildings and conditions in schools. Parents, teachers, workers and other citizens came out in support of students. Officials estimated 5.5 lakh demonstrators nationwide, while organisers claimed around 8 lakh. The two counts have different sources.

The report distinguishes peaceful marches from separate incidents of arson, vandalism and looting. Shops and public buildings were damaged in several cities. The government blamed hard-left groups and looters for the violence. Opposition groups also questioned police action and the handling of protests.

President Emmanuel Macron was due to address the nation on Sunday night. The live page consulted was still awaiting that address, so no claim about its outcome is made here. The government had already spoken of extra substitute teachers and relief on some fees. But broader demands concerning public services, budgets and rising prices remained. Both the reasons for the protests and the investigation into violence are central to the next political steps.
nazar: While responsibility for violence is established, peaceful protesters' demands should be heard separately. Continually changing counts should not be presented as final truths either.
Students' demand for safe, functioning schools should have been heard before it became a major political crisis.
sawal: Will the question of schools survive the images of violence?
ref: Live report
A news page continually updated with new information, where counts recorded at different times may change.

h: Kolkata pandal disaster: 7 arrested as safety is investigated
dek: Maktoob's latest report details an investigation into crowd management and organisers' responsibility after 19 deaths.
body: Police arrested 7 people over deaths caused by crowd pressure and a stampede at Kolkata's Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal on 17 October. According to Maktoob's report of 18 October, 19 people had died and 25 were injured. Many of those who died were reported to be women and children.

Quoting a senior police officer, the report identifies sudden rain, shortcomings in crowd management and confusing announcements as possible causes of the chaos. These are preliminary investigative findings. They cannot yet be treated as final conclusions about the disaster's full causes or different individuals' responsibility. The investigation is examining arrangements for the event and safety preparations.

Those arrested include Puja committee officeholders, a person connected to construction, crowd-control staff and people responsible for private security. Earlier, 14 people had been questioned. Police registered a case on their own initiative at Girish Park police station. Officials say questioning continues over alleged shortcomings in crowd management, safety rules and structural arrangements.

The report also mentions the chief minister's announcement of an inquiry supervised by a sitting High Court judge. The prime minister announced assistance of Rs 2 lakh for bereaved families and Rs 50,000 for the injured. Announcing assistance and establishing safety accountability are separate tasks. It remains to be seen how clearly the inquiry examines the entire organisation of the event and how affected families receive that information.
nazar: Calling a crowd disaster merely a sudden panic narrows the scope of responsibility. Entrances, exits, preparations for rain and announcement systems must be part of the inquiry.
Compensation can provide relief; to save the next life, the inquiry's findings must be made public and implemented.
sawal: Which safety rules will change before the next event?
ref: Crowd management
Advance arrangements to keep entrances, exits, routes and the number of people safe.

h: Medals on the mat, another struggle for a living outside
dek: For judo players arriving in Pune from villages, training, study and earning a living go together.
body: Young people arriving at Pune's judo training centres from villages and small towns carry more than dreams of medals. For many, sport is also a route to improving their family's finances and securing a government job. Ankita Kumari's report reveals the other work behind the training of players such as Soham Kamble and Payal Gilda: covering their expenses in the city.

Soham came to Pune from Indapur for better training. He works in deliveries to pay rent, food costs and training fees. His family earns from farming and a small shop, but staying in the city without regular support is difficult. The hope that a medal will bring a job and security for the family increases the pressure to win.

Payal, from Beed, has participated in several sports. Her mother runs a shop, and her family has supported her education and sport. Scholarships and offsetting fees by training younger children help. Yet Payal says she learned about some sports support schemes too late, after she had passed their age limit.

The report shows both the usefulness of government training schemes and gaps in their reach. Some assistance reaches athletes who are already successful, while those struggling at an early stage need that help most. The difficulties of moving from a village to a city, obtaining reliable information and maintaining training while earning a living show that identifying talent and sustaining it are different tasks.
nazar: Equality in sport means more than one set of rules on the field. Information, nutrition, accommodation and early financial assistance also determine opportunity.
Turning the success of athletes who must choose between work and training solely into a story of personal determination conceals shortcomings in public provision.
sawal: Will help come before a medal, or always afterwards?
ref: Krida Prabodhini
A government-supported system in Maharashtra that provides training and other assistance to young athletes.

h: Rural livelihoods and unease at Delhi's sit-in
dek: In Shadab Farooq's report, daily-wage workers, migrants and students join the movement for their own reasons.
body: Delhi's protest did not belong only to the capital's students. Shadab Farooq's photographs and conversations show daily-wage workers from Hardoi, a graduate from Jhansi, a migrant from a village and an urban worker holding several jobs on a low income. Reaching the movement meant more than expressing a political opinion for them; it also meant setting aside part of their time and limited earnings.

Daya Shankar and his companion Chhakkoo travelled a long distance from Hardoi to Delhi and spent the night on the pavement. Shankar connects his protest to social solidarity. He expresses exhaustion with divisive politics and believes standing with another family today could mean support for his own family tomorrow. His words give the report a foundation apart from leaders' platforms.

Yadram sells clothes during the day and drives an app-based vehicle at night. He says the names of 3 women in his family have been removed from the electoral roll. This is his recorded statement, not the conclusion of an independent examination of the entire list. The experience of this Dalit family, which moved from Rajasthan to Delhi, shows how administrative procedures affect citizens' everyday trust.

The report includes experiences of heavy police deployment, restrictions on movement and people still trying to reach the protest. Some students also alleged beatings and the compulsion to conceal their identities. Farooq records these voices on their own ground. Amid the broader dispute over the Election Commission and protest, this report reminds us that even the lowest-income citizen pays the cost of political demands through time, fares and lost wages.
nazar: It would be wrong to lose rural participation in a movement within a simple headcount. The cost of travel and missed daily wages is also part of democratic participation.
Every complaint about a removed name should be investigated with the individual concerned. A family's actual routes of appeal and restoration must not disappear in the larger debate over numbers.
sawal: Who counts the daily wages lost by coming to protest?
ref: Migrant labour
Work undertaken after moving from one's home village or state to another place for employment.

h: Salaya's sailors, war in the Gulf and shattered livelihoods
dek: In Gujarat's shipbuilding and trading settlement, war has affected lives, savings and futures.
body: Salaya, in Gujarat's Dwarka district, is known for large handmade wooden ships and maritime work. Marhaba Hilali's report says 2 cargo ships from here were destroyed in missile attacks during the Iran-US war. For sailors who survived and returned, the story does not end with escaping the sea. Earnings, documents and confidence in returning to work have also been lost.

Nazir Junas Bhaya was aboard the ship attacked in May. According to his account, a companion died and survivors stayed afloat in the sea for hours. Nazir lost his savings, passport and seafarer's identity document. The report presents his suspicion about the attacker's identity as his statement; it is not treated here as a confirmed conclusion.

Aijaz and his companions, who survived from the other ship, are also afraid to go to sea again. Shipowners complain of not receiving insurance payments or relief. Building and operating ships, and loading and unloading cargo, are major sources of work in this settlement. Where education and other local opportunities are limited, surviving a war and returning home does not guarantee financial security.

The report also visits families who returned from work in Dubai, where job losses and restrictions affected children's education. Salaya's women are used to long separations at sea, but the risk of war is different. Published in August, this report records young sailors' dilemma: stay away to save their lives, or return to the same uncertain sea to meet the needs of their homes, debts and families.
nazar: The local cost of a distant war can be found in settlements like this. Restoring sailors' documents, insurance and protection for family incomes cannot be separated from foreign-policy discussions.
This is an August report. The losses it records should not be read as a new event that happened today.
sawal: Who will protect the livelihood of a sailor returning from war?
ref: Dhow
A traditional wooden seagoing vessel long used in Indian Ocean trade.

h: A Bhoodan title in Guna, but incomplete rights on the ground
dek: Satish Malaviya shows the gap between paperwork and actual possession in Adivasi families' land disputes.
body: Many Adivasi (indigenous) families in Guna, Madhya Pradesh, have papers for Bhoodan land, but their actual ownership remains unclear. Satish Malaviya's report connects this unfulfilled promise to local struggles and violence. The absence of demarcation showing who claims which part of village land leaves vulnerable families continually insecure.

Galsingh Bhilala had told the reporter that others occupied land allotted to his ancestors and revenue officials had not clarified the situation. He was later attacked over a land dispute and died. The report also records violent clashes between the Bhilala and Banjara communities and the condition of displaced families. Blaming one community for all the disputes does not explain their layers.

Mandya Bhilala's family came here decades ago in search of work and food. He says land they received was later taken back. The report makes clear that it has no documentary evidence of this confiscation during the Emergency. This caution matters: the family's memories, government records and present ownership require separate investigation.

Even after the Forest Rights Act, many families keep visiting offices for titles and secure cultivation rights. Complaints of water shortages and pressure from influential people make their livelihoods harder. This July report shows that announcing land distribution does not automatically bring justice. Without clear records, demarcation, actual possession and protection for vulnerable claimants, an old promise can remain a dispute for generations.
nazar: Land reform cannot be fully assessed merely by counting titles distributed. The real test is whether titleholders can cultivate the land.
Leaving communities to fight one another without clarifying the separate Bhoodan and forest-rights procedures evades administrative accountability.
sawal: If there is a title, why is there no security on the land?
ref: Bhoodan movement
A movement initiated by Vinoba Bhave to obtain land from large landowners and give it to landless people.
Demarcation
Determining a plot's actual boundaries and location on the ground according to records.

h: On Gaza's road, searching for a family
dek: Separated by war for over a year, a family returns after the ceasefire, but uncertainty about contact and the journey remains.
by: Mohammed Sawwaf, Salah Al-Haw, Ibrahim Al-Otla and Mohammed Masharawi
body: Captain Momin of Gaza's Civil Defence has been separated from his family for more than a year during the war. Al Jazeera Witness's film Gaza Family Reunion centres on the attempt to meet again. Its published description offers a way of seeing the war's effects through a family's journey and waiting, rather than through a major diplomatic announcement.

According to the description, Momin's wife and children leave Nuseirat refugee camp the day after a ceasefire is announced. They had been staying there to escape relentless bombing. Now they must return north, where Momin is waiting. The possibility of returning home has opened, but reunion after a long separation has still not become automatic.

Carrying their remaining belongings on their backs, the family walks along Gaza's long coastal road. They must travel over difficult ground among large numbers of returning people. The film's description places the movement of hundreds of thousands of people alongside the difficulty of finding one small family. The private meaning of a public announcement emerges in this way through roads, belongings and physical exhaustion.

Momin is at the other end of the route. There is no phone signal, and locating his wife and children in the crowd becomes difficult. Being able to call a loved one seems a small convenience in ordinary times. Here, its absence increases waiting and uncertainty. The description shows that war's effects lie not only in displacement but also in the breakdown of communication and trust.

This introduction is based on the film's official page and description. No unseen scenes, dialogue or final outcome of the family's reunion have therefore been added here. The film is by Mohammed Sawwaf, Salah Al-Haw, Ibrahim Al-Otla and Mohammed Masharawi. Readers can watch the original film below to encounter this journey and waiting in its own form.
nazar: Judging a ceasefire through citizens' eyes begins with this question: can families meet safely, return home and speak to one another?
Momin's waiting brings into view an ordinary right hidden beneath grand political language: reaching a loved one should not put one's life at risk.
sawal: How safe is returning home after a ceasefire?
ref: Civil Defence
A service providing rescue, firefighting and civilian assistance in emergencies.
Nuseirat
A refugee camp in central Gaza where many displaced families also stayed during the war.

h: A character asks his author for freedom
dek: Basant Tripathi's story Mukti questions creative authority, the writer's ego and a character's own wishes.
body: We readily assume that an author decides what happens to a character. In Basant Tripathi's story Mukti (Liberation), the character challenges this arrangement. He has already gone to court seeking release from the author and now tells the story from his own side. Here, the creator himself becomes a character under scrutiny.

The narrator has no permanent name. The writer has kept assigning him different roles in different stories, gaining fame and awards with his help. The character's complaint is not just about credit but about control over his existence. His own wishes have had no place in decisions about when to wake him, where to bring him and how to make him behave.

The story exposes the distance between a writer's public image of sensitivity and conduct in private life. The extent to which someone who writes about love and women's freedom can be authoritarian in personal relationships is a sharp focus of its satire. As the conflict between writer and character grows, the character begins refusing to perform assigned roles.

The effect of this reversal extends beyond literature. Turning someone into an instrument of one's own story, claiming to speak for them while taking away their wishes, appears in many forms of power. Mukti questions the point where someone's livelihood and subordination are tied together. The story's pleasure lies in its narrator's mischievous interventions and the continuing collapse of the writer's arrangements.
nazar: Giving a character a voice and allowing him to speak of his own will are different tasks. The story carries this question from the author to the reader.
Claims of social commitment will be tested not only through a work's subject, but also through whether its outlook treats another human as an instrument or an equal person.
sawal: When the character begins speaking, how much does the writer listen?
ref: Self-aware fiction
A story that also discusses its own creation, the narrator and the author's role.

h: What did Apsara receive while tending the household's hunger?
dek: In her memories, Neha Naruka connects the neglect of one woman to the larger structure of family and society.
body: In this instalment of Neha Naruka's series Mritatmaon Ka Desh (Land of Dead Souls), a woman named Apsara returns through memories told by the family. The writer never saw her, yet surviving accounts of her life remain in the writer's own consciousness. Rather than recording family memories unchanged, this writing reads the injustices hidden within them that have been accepted as normal.

The most readily remembered thing about Apsara is how much she ate. Yet the same memory reveals that she understood others' hunger too, especially that of the household's daughters-in-law. The woman described as eating leftovers also fed others in secret. The article draws attention to how family language diminishes her wishes and generosity.

In accounts of marriage and illness, neither her home, her marital home nor the place of treatment offers her full belonging. With bitter satire, the writer exposes calculations that remember wedding expenses before a girl's health. A bench outside a hospital becomes both shelter and a place of homelessness. What is a desire for freedom for one woman can be a need for warmth and a roof during illness for another.

The work repeatedly returns to the act of writing itself. Telling Apsara's story is not easy mourning for the writer; it is a recognition that parts of old injustices reach girls today. The tree and domestic memories left after her death do not remain merely sentimental symbols. They ask in what form a family remembers a woman and how fully it confronts her actual suffering.
nazar: This publicly published memoir turns private pain into a social question. Its force lies in recognising cruelty hidden in ordinary domestic language rather than in sensationalising an incident.
A family's claim to care for a woman should be tested through its behaviour concerning her illness, food and accommodation.
sawal: Where are a woman's own wishes in the family's memory?
ref: Memoir writing
Writing that reads past experiences and inherited family memories through the writer's present understanding.

h: Who gets a place to live in the city they came to study in?
dek: Durgesh Kumar Sajal's satire exposes the social screening hidden in the search for a rented room.
body: Admission to college secured, but no room to live in. Durgesh Kumar Sajal's satire begins with this second entrance examination for a student. Searching through lanes for a room introduces him to a social structure whose lessons differ from those in books. In some places, being a student is itself grounds for suspicion; elsewhere, having a job is treated as proof of respectability.

Landlords' questions begin to cover much more than rent and space. Who will visit, when will you return, what will you eat, whom will you meet and what is your full name? Such questions stake a claim over a tenant's private life. Attempts to identify caste behind names and surnames are present too. The satire catches the screening concealed within this ordinary conversation.

The piece mocks the moral superiority automatically granted by age and social standing. People who praise education can humiliate young people who come to their doors to study. The gap between leniency for their own children and strict rules for others also emerges. Renting a room gradually becomes an attempt to control a person's entire life.

The work uses exaggeration and biting comparisons, so it should not be treated as a survey of all landlords. Its value lies in making a recurring experience public. Without hostel accommodation, a student can be left alone between the market and social prejudice. A discussion of access to education remains incomplete when safe, dignified accommodation is not counted as part of it.
nazar: Opportunity at university does not end with an admission letter. Rent, caste screening, food preferences and restrictions on movement determine who can continue studying.
The satire's anger is useful, but solutions also require hostels, written rental agreements and credible grievance systems against discrimination.
sawal: Admission secured, but where is a place to live with dignity?
ref: Housing discrimination
Refusing someone a rental home or imposing different conditions because of identity, caste, religion, gender or lifestyle.

h: The protest reel and the viewer's responsibility
dek: Rachit reads humour, participation and the distant spectator's comfort together in protest's digital fairground.
body: Rachit begins his commentary by comparing a movement to a fair. People with different skills, habits and voices meet in a public gathering. Alongside older forms such as songs, spinning wheels, clowning and speeches, mobile reels have now appeared. For the writer, this presence does not automatically prove that a movement is unserious. The methods of public politics are changing.

He observes popular faces usually confined to the worlds of entertainment or jokes. Their arrival at a movement can bring in different audiences. The writer examines his own surprise too: why do we find it difficult to regard someone who makes reels as a politically serious citizen? This question exposes the viewer's own hierarchies.

In viral videos of people running from police, anxiety, humour and recognition come together. A small incident can suddenly reach many people. But Rachit also asks who came for the movement and who came for the reel. Drawing a firm wall between the two is difficult because digital images have themselves become a means of political participation and shaping public opinion.

The commentary's most uncomfortable turn is towards the spectator sitting at home. The person watching a movement on screen and explaining its meaning is personally far from the risk. The writer does not exempt his own role from this comfort either. The work does not end by praising or condemning reels. It asks how direct our knowledge is when describing struggles on the ground, and whether someone else is paying the price for our lack of worry.
nazar: Deciding an entire movement's direction or character from a viral fragment is an easy but weak conclusion. Short videos must be read with context and other sources.
Offering an opinion from a distance is not wrong, but recognising that distance and the limits of one's knowledge is its first act of honesty.
sawal: Whose risk disappears from view while we watch a reel?
ref: Viral video
A short video that reaches large numbers of people through sharing; popularity is not proof of its truth.

h: In Shivani's towns, looking for an address for her memory
dek: Abhishek Kumar Ambar looks for Shivani's presence and erasure between her writing and homes in the hills.
body: Abhishek Kumar Ambar reads Shivani by moving between her writing and the actual places associated with her. On a journey through Almora and Nainital, memories of books show the way, but the towns do not always preserve those memories. A changed house or people nearby who do not recognise the writer creates a distance between literature and public memory.

Women such as Rajula, their songs and the lives preserved in Shivani's stories accompany this journey. The writer does not turn the stories merely into introductions to places to visit. He asks how much we would know about the women whose pain and skills found space in the writing if their voices had not been recorded. Literature becomes another kind of social record here.

The search for Prairie Lodge in Nainital brings different accounts of local history, family property and altered buildings. In some places the old house is gone; in others the name is unknown. The writer's search does not end at a ready-made memorial. Having to keep asking for the address of a memory shows how quickly a famous writer's town can remove her from its everyday life.

The article's tone is shaped by travel, a reader's affection and dissatisfaction. It sees hill society present in Shivani's works and then asks how that same society has remembered her. The availability of books and the presence of memory in a town are not the same thing. Houses, roads and readers together make a writer's living legacy, which can gradually disappear without care.
nazar: Preserving a writer's home means more than installing a statue or sign. Readings, local people's memories and public access can make it a useful place.
Alongside Shivani's memory, the voices of the ordinary women who formed the world of her writing should also survive.
sawal: Who preserved in the town the town preserved in books?
ref: Shivani
Gaura Pant's pen name; her stories and novels contain a distinctive world of the hills and women's lives.

h: Starting in the middle, taking another route to memory
dek: In Vinod Chandola's translation, Anne Carson's poems and conversation free writing from a fixed beginning.
body: This Sadaneera selection brings Anne Carson's poems and a conversation together. Vinod Chandola's Hindi translation presents experiences of memory, love and loss. An everyday object, such as a father's old garment, becomes a route to someone's absence and the habits they have left behind. The complete poems should be read on the original page.

Time does not move forward in a straight line in these works. The shadow of a past day can appear within another day, and an ordinary domestic scene can open a deep feeling. Readers receive more than an account of an event; they see how memory changes present experience. Metaphor and the movement of sentences matter in this recognition.

In the accompanying conversation, ordinary matters such as the kitchen, tea and sweeping the floor appear amid news of a major literary honour. Carson does not compress her writing into a weighty declaration. She advises someone looking for a beginning to start working in the middle. Rather than treating this as a ready-made technique, it can be understood as her way of entering uncertainty.

In a question about Homer and classical literature too, she reverses the usual demand for relevance. Alongside asking whether an old work is useful today, we can ask what kind of readers we are before it. Placing poems and conversation together opens another form of seriousness: continuing to work on one's art without imposing a final formula, and keeping the stir of ordinary life connected to writing.
nazar: A writer's experience need not always be turned into an orderly life story. An object, an incomplete memory or a line from the middle can also be a route to truth.
This freedom is no excuse for vagueness. While reading, we must ask whether even a fragmented form gives the reader a precise experience.
sawal: Must every story begin at the beginning?
ref: Homer
The poet-name associated with the ancient Greek epics the Iliad and the Odyssey, whose works Carson repeatedly engages with.
